newsitem.title: USA: ASARCO reiterates copper deficits ahead.
newsitem.headline: ASARCO reiterates copper deficits ahead.

text.p: ASARCO, the world's fourth largest non state-owned copper company, reiterated that the Western world's copper market will remain in deficit this year and next, despite the onslaught of new supplies, including more metal from the company itself.

ASARCO chairman Richard de J Osborne told the company's annual meeting in New York Wednesday that following last year's western world copper market deficit of 172,000 short tons, further estimated deficits of 53,000 short tons and 149,000 short tons will be notched up in 1997 and 1998 respectively.

Copper inventories were already down to 2.6 weeks of supply, with a further 1.5 weeks in transit. Any hiccup in production will have an immediate effect. "There is no buffer," Osborne told reporters after the meeting.

ASARCO, which produced just over a billion pounds of copper (453,600 tonnes) in 1996, went out on a limb last year by predicting market deficits for 1997 and 1998 while a gaggle of analysts predicted growing surpluses from the end of 1996.
But Osborne felt less lonely is predicting deficits as some analysts were now more bullish and expected delays in the arrival of surpluses.
"Generally people are pushing the (supply) bubble ahead, but really the bubble is behind us," Osborne said.
Twice the amount of extra copper came on stream between 1993 and last year compared with what is set to hit the market over the next few years, Osborne said.
Demand was continually being understated, and consumption in the Western world was forecast to rise 3.4 percent this year and next, setting new records and drawing down inventories.
Copper consumption this year and next will be an estimated 12,097,000 tons and 12,505,000 tons respectively, ASARCO forecast.
"But I think copper still carries a lot of negativism from the analysts, but there seems to be fewer of them," Osborne.

He added that poor copper data from organizations such as the American Bureau of Metal Statistics, which recently revised downwards Western world copper inventories by some 200,000 tons, was partly to blame for forecasts of surpluses in the past.
Osborne said he still had no confidence in some data gathering which relied too much on estimating.

The company's 75 percent owned Silver Bell mine and solvent extraction, electrowinning plant in Arizona comes on stream in July with annual output of 36 million pounds of copper in cathode at cash costs of 50 cents per pound. Mitsui of Japan owns the rest of the project.
ASARCO's current cash costs are 65 to 70 cents per pound. COMEX spot copper closed at 112.50 cents on Wednesday.

Osborne also expected the copper smelter bottleneck, which caused refining charges to soar to about 40 cents per pound last year, will move into balance by the end of this year with refining charges dropping further from current levels of 30-35 cents.
Osborne declined to comment on second quarter results outlook, saying too much depended on the price of copper.
Plunging copper prices last year shaved $187 million off earnings and each 1 cent move in copper price triggers a 16 cent net change in annual earnings per share.
